sources: canada.ca CRA 'Canada workers benefit – How much you can get' · 2025 · family basic maximum $2,813; reduced by 15% of adjusted family net income above $30,639; nil above $49,393; a single parent with an eligible dependant uses the family amounts
CRA What's new for 2025 · 2025 · lowest federal rate 14.5% for 2025 (15% to June 30, 14% from July 1); basic personal amount $16,129; first bracket to $57,375
canada.ca CRA 'Canada child benefit – How much you can get' · July 2026–June 2027 (2025 income) · reduction 7% for one child on adjusted family net income above $38,237
canada.ca CRA Canada Groceries and Essentials Benefit · July 2026–June 2027 · 5% phase-out above $46,432 (no change in this example)

Calculation (not a CRA rule): m17/data.json. Maya, single parent, one child, 2025: $24,000 → $40,000. Federal: $16,000 × 14.5% = $2,320. CWB: $2,813 − 15% × ($40,000 − $30,639) = $1,408.85 → −$1,404.15 (full $2,813 at $24,000, assuming the basic amount is fully phased in). CCB: 7% × ($40,000 − $38,237) = $123.41/yr from July 2026. Total $3,847.56 (24.0%); kept $12,152.44. On dollars between $38,237 and $40,000: 14.5% + 15% + 7% = 36.5%. Provincial tax, CPP and EI not included.

yt.description:
Maya went full-time: $16,000 more a year. Almost $4,000 of it never reaches her.

Single parent, one child, 2025: $24,000 part-time → $40,000 full-time.
• Federal tax: 14.5% of the extra = $2,320
• Canada Workers Benefit: shrinks 15% above $30,639 → −$1,404
• Canada Child Benefit: 7% above $38,237, from July 2026 → −$123
= −$3,848 (24%). She keeps $12,152.

The twist: on her last dollars, about 36 cents of each one is gone, before provincial tax, CPP and EI.

Before you switch, count the benefits, not just the paycheque.

Next: why January's paycheque shrinks. Follow so you don't miss it.

Sources: canada.ca (CRA) CWB how much you can get (2025); What's new for 2025; CCB how much you can get (July 2026–June 2027). Example, federal only; general information, not tax advice.
